title: Print Statements
summary: Write your first Go program and print text with fmt.Println and fmt.Print.
intro: Every Go program talks to you through its output. You will write the skeleton every Go program shares, then print lines, pieces of lines, and special characters with the `fmt` package.

steps.title: Your first program
steps.body:
Every Go program is a file that starts with `package main`, imports the packages it uses, and defines `func main()`. The program starts running at the first line of `main` and stops when `main` ends.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	// fmt.Println writes one line
	fmt.Println("Hello, Go!")
}
```

`import "fmt"` brings in the formatting package that holds the print functions.

`fmt.Println("text")` prints its text, then ends the line, so the next call starts on a new one. Text goes in double quotes. Single quotes do not make a string in Go.

A `//` comment runs to the end of the line and is ignored by the compiler.

Go has one standard layout, the one `gofmt` prints: tabs for indentation and the opening brace on the same line as `func main()`. Putting the brace on its own line is a compile error, not just a style choice. Never use the builtin `println`: it writes to stderr, not to normal output.

example.title: Welcome banner
example.prompt: Print a three line welcome banner with one `fmt.Println` call per line.
example.output:
Welcome to Hack University
Lesson 1: printing
Let's write some Go!
example.explanation: The program starts at the top of `main`. Each `fmt.Println` call prints its string and ends the line, so three calls make three lines, in the order they run. The comment changes nothing in the output.

practice.title: Course card
practice.prompt:
Print a three line course card.

1. Print `Course: Go Basics` (the starter already does this).
2. Print `Level: Beginner`.
3. Print `Status: Enrolled`.

Expected output:

```text
Course: Go Basics
Level: Beginner
Status: Enrolled
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println("Course: Go Basics")
	fmt.Println("Level: Beginner")
	fmt.Println("Status: Enrolled")
}

tests.output:
Course: Go Basics
Level: Beginner
Status: Enrolled

hints: Use one `fmt.Println` call per line, just like the first one.
Put each new call on its own line inside `main`, indented with a tab, and copy the text exactly, including the colon and the space after it.

steps.title: Several values and fmt.Print
steps.body:
`fmt.Println` takes any number of arguments separated by commas. It prints them with a single space between each one and ends the line. Called with no arguments, it prints an empty line.

```go
fmt.Println("red", "green", "blue") // red green blue
fmt.Println()                        // empty line
```

`fmt.Print` prints its text but does **not** end the line, so the next print continues on the same line. It also adds no spaces between strings, so put any spaces inside the quotes yourself.

To end a line with `fmt.Print`, put the newline escape `\n` inside the string. The two characters `\n` stand for one newline character.

```go
fmt.Print("one, ")
fmt.Print("two\n") // one, two
```

Use `fmt.Println` for whole lines and `fmt.Print` when you build one line from several pieces. If you forget the final `\n`, the next output lands on the end of that line.

example.title: Ready, set, go
example.prompt: Print a sentence from three arguments, an empty line, then one line built from three `fmt.Print` calls.
example.output:
Go is fun

Ready, set, go!
example.explanation: `fmt.Println("Go", "is", "fun")` puts one space between the three strings and ends the line. `fmt.Println()` with no arguments prints just a line break, which shows up as an empty line. The three `fmt.Print` calls write `Ready, `, `set, ` and `go!` side by side, and the `\n` at the end of the last string finishes the line.

practice.title: Launch countdown
practice.prompt:
Print a sentence, an empty line, and a countdown built piece by piece.

1. Print `Hack University rocks` with one `fmt.Println` call that takes three arguments.
2. Print an empty line (the starter already does this).
3. Print `3, 2, 1, launch!` with four `fmt.Print` calls, ending the last string with `\n`.

Expected output:

```text
Hack University rocks

3, 2, 1, launch!
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println("Hack", "University", "rocks")
	fmt.Println()
	fmt.Print("3, ")
	fmt.Print("2, ")
	fmt.Print("1, ")
	fmt.Print("launch!\n")
}
hints: `fmt.Println` adds the spaces between its arguments, so pass `"Hack"`, `"University"` and `"rocks"` with no spaces inside the quotes.
`fmt.Print` adds nothing, so keep the comma and space inside each piece: `fmt.Print("3, ")`.
Only the last piece needs `\n`, so the line ends after `launch!`.

steps.title: Escapes and raw strings
steps.body:
Inside double quotes, a backslash starts an escape sequence:

- `\n` is a newline and `\t` is a tab, handy for lining up columns.
- `\"` is a double quote that does not end the string.
- `\\` is one backslash.

That last one matters for paths. In `"C:\temp"` the `\t` is a tab, so it prints `C:` and a tab followed by `emp`. Write `"C:\\temp"` instead. A backslash before a letter that is not an escape, as in `"C:\go"`, does not compile at all. The compiler reports `unknown escape`.

A **raw string** goes between backticks. It ignores escapes, so `\n` stays two characters, and it can span several lines:

```go
fmt.Println(`line one
line two \n stays as is`)
```

A raw string keeps every character between its backticks, indentation included. So even inside an indented `main`, start its second and later lines at column 0, or the tabs become part of the text. A raw string cannot contain a backtick.

example.title: Menu, quote, and box
example.prompt: Print a tab-separated menu, a quote, a Windows path, and a three line box from one raw string.
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println("Item\tPrice")
	fmt.Println("Tea\t2")
	fmt.Println("She said \"hi\"")
	// Without \\ the \t and \n here would become a tab and a newline
	fmt.Println("Saved to C:\\temp\\notes.txt")
	fmt.Println(`+--------+
| Hi, Go |
+--------+`)
}
example.output:
Item	Price
Tea	2
She said "hi"
Saved to C:\temp\notes.txt
+--------+
| Hi, Go |
+--------+
example.explanation: `\t` puts a tab between the columns, and the terminal lines `Price` and `2` up at the next tab stop. `\"` prints a quote without ending the string. Each `\\` prints one backslash, so the path keeps its `\t` and `\n` as text. The box is one raw string: its newlines are real line breaks in the source, and its second and third lines start at column 0 so no tabs sneak into the output.

practice.title: Score sheet
practice.prompt:
Print a small score sheet with escapes and finish with an arrow drawn in a raw string.

1. Print `Name` and `Score` separated by a tab (the starter already does this).
2. Print `Ada` and `95` separated by a tab.
3. Print the path `C:\go\bin`, writing each backslash as `\\`.
4. Print `Type "go run" to start`, using `\"` for the quotes.
5. Print the three line arrow below with one `fmt.Println` of a backtick raw string. The first line starts with two spaces, the second with one, the third with two.

Expected output:

```text
Name	Score
Ada	95
C:\go\bin
Type "go run" to start
  ^
 /|\
  |
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println("Name\tScore")
	fmt.Println("Ada\t95")
	fmt.Println("C:\\go\\bin")
	fmt.Println("Type \"go run\" to start")
	fmt.Println(`  ^
 /|\
  |`)
}

tests.output:
Name	Score
Ada	95
C:\go\bin
Type "go run" to start
  ^
 /|\
  |

hints: Copy the header line and change the text: `"Ada\t95"`.
Inside double quotes a single `\` starts an escape, so the path needs `\\` twice.
Inside backticks the `\` in the arrow is just a backslash. Start the arrow's second and third lines at column 0, with only the spaces the drawing needs.

recap:
- Every program has `package main`, `import "fmt"`, and `func main()`, where it starts.
- `fmt.Println("a", "b")` prints its arguments joined by spaces and ends the line. `fmt.Println()` prints an empty line.
- `fmt.Print` does not end the line or put spaces between strings, so add spaces and `\n` yourself.
- Escapes in double quotes: `\n` newline, `\t` tab, `\"` quote, `\\` backslash.
- Backtick raw strings ignore escapes and span lines. Start their later lines at column 0.
- Use tabs and keep the opening brace on the same line. Never use the builtin `println`.
